c.tagline: Shipyard city reborn — Titanic heritage, murals, and warm craic.

taxi.fareNote: Uber operates in Belfast but with limited driver numbers, so waits can be long; most people book by app or phone through fonaCAB or Value Cabs. The famous black-cab political mural tours run as separate guided tours, not as metered rides.

emergency.note: 999 is the UK all-services emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 112 also works.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Very safe for visitors; some interface/"peace-wall" areas (Falls/Shankill) sensitive but visited by day

hood_desc: Belfast's cobbled arts and nightlife heart around St Anne's Cathedral, packed with traditional pubs, live-music bars, galleries, and street murals; best for visitors who want to be out among the craic.
The convenient walkable core around City Hall and the Linen Quarter, close to shopping on Donegall Place and Victoria Square and most transport links; the easiest first-timer base.
The cultural district radiating from red-brick Queen's University, home to the Ulster Museum, Botanic Gardens, and student-priced cafes; suits culture-seekers wanting good value near the sights.
The regenerated waterfront where the Titanic was built, dominated by the Titanic Belfast museum, the SS Nomadic, and the Harland & Wolff cranes; great for families and maritime-history buffs.
A leafy, studenty avenue of Victorian terraces, guesthouses, and casual eateries just south of the centre near the university; a calmer, budget-friendly place to stay.
lodging: Premier Inn Belfast City Centre (Alfred Street)
Residence Inn by Marriott Belfast Titanic Quarter

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Northern Ireland.

transit.hours: Metro buses and the Glider run roughly 6am-11:30pm, with Nightmover late buses on Friday and Saturday nights; trains run about 6am-11pm.
transit.note: Belfast is served by Translink's Glider bus rapid transit, Metro city buses, and NI Railways local trains; there is no metro or tram.
transit.pay: Tap a contactless bank card or phone on Glider and Metro buses, or buy a paper ticket from the driver (cash) or a smart mLink/iLink card. A single Glider/Metro fare is about £2.20; a day ticket is around £3.60. Trains use separate tickets or the iLink smartcard.

ferry: Belfast Ferry Terminal (Stena Line to Cairnryan)

transit.m: Airport Express 300 bus to Europa Buscentre (~40 min, every 15-30 min)

tip.r: Service is not automatically added; around 10% for good restaurant service is customary, and rounding up is normal for taxis and pubs.

food.name: Ulster fry

places.name: Maggie May's
places.note: Student-priced Belfast institution widely rated for the full Ulster fry.

places.name: Cafe Conor

places.note: Airy former artist's studio serving a well-made fry all morning.

places.name: General Merchants
places.note: Modern brunch spot that does a lighter, sharper take on the fry.

food.name: Soda farl and potato bread
food.desc: Griddle breads unique to Ulster: a soft quartered soda farl and a thin, floury potato bread, best eaten hot with butter or fried in the fry.

places.name: St George's Market bakery stalls
places.note: Friday-to-Sunday market where local bakers sell farls straight off the griddle.

places.name: Belfast Bap Company
places.note: Market favourite building huge breakfast baps on fresh local breads.

places.name: Maggie May's
places.note: Farls and potato bread come as standard with every breakfast plate.

food.name: Champ
food.desc: Buttery mashed potato beaten through with scallions and a well of melted butter in the middle; the plainest and most beloved Ulster side.

places.name: The Garrick Bar

places.note: Old-school city pub widely said to serve the best champ in Belfast.

places.name: The Crown Liquor Saloon

places.name: Mourne Seafood Bar
places.note: Serves champ alongside County Down fish and shellfish.

food.name: Irish stew and steak-and-Guinness pie
food.desc: Slow-cooked lamb or beef with root vegetables, or beef braised in stout under pastry; the standard warming plate in Belfast's older bars.

places.name: Kelly's Cellars
places.note: Belfast's oldest pub, from 1720, known for stew and afternoon trad sessions.

places.name: The Crown Liquor Saloon
places.note: National Trust-owned Victorian bar, famous enough to be worth the queue.

places.name: The Duke of York
places.note: Lantern-lit cobbled alley pub with hearty food and huge whiskey shelves.

food.desc: Oysters, mussels and crab from the loughs and the County Down coast an hour away, landed daily and served simply with soda bread.

places.note: Belfast's best-known seafood room, with its own shellfish beds in Co Down.

places.note: Michelin-starred chef's more casual fish restaurant in the city centre.

places.name: St George's Market fish rows

food.name: Yellowman
food.desc: Brittle golden honeycomb toffee of brown sugar, syrup and vinegar, traditionally sold at the Ould Lammas Fair and still made along the Antrim coast.

places.name: St George's Market sweet stalls
places.note: Weekend stalls sell slabs of yellowman alongside other Ulster sweets.

places.name: Local sweet shops in the city centre

places.name: The Crown Liquor Saloon
places.note: Gas-lit tiled snugs from 1826; Anthony Bourdain rated it Belfast's best pub.

places.name: Kelly's Cellars
places.note: Whitewashed 1720 bar, low ceilings, trad music and a proper pint.

places.name: The Duke of York

food.desc: Bushmills from the north Antrim coast plus a wave of new local distillers; Belfast bars now keep whiskey lists that run to hundreds of bottles.

landmarks: Titanic Belfast
An aluminium-clad museum shaped like ship prows rises on the very slipways where RMS Titanic was built, telling the liner's story with theatrical flair.
Belfast City Hall
This exuberant Edwardian Baroque palace of Portland stone dominates Donegall Square, its copper domes, marble interiors and memorial gardens open for free guided tours.
Peace Walls and Political Murals
Black-cab tours trace the towering peace lines and vivid murals of the Falls and Shankill Roads, an open-air chronicle of the Troubles and reconciliation.
Crumlin Road Gaol
A grimly fascinating Victorian prison that held suffragettes, loyalists and republicans for 150 years, now offering tours of its tunnel, cells and execution chamber.
St Anne's Cathedral (Belfast Cathedral)
Belfast's Hiberno-Romanesque Anglican cathedral anchors the buzzing Cathedral Quarter, its slender stainless-steel Spire of Hope piercing the skyline above intricate mosaics.
Cave Hill and Belfast Castle
The basalt crag said to have inspired Gulliver's Travels looms over the city, with a baronial Victorian castle and summit views across Belfast Lough.
Botanic Gardens and Palm House
Beside Queen's University, these Victorian gardens shelter a curvilinear cast-iron Palm House of 1840, one of the earliest glasshouses of its kind anywhere.
Ulster Museum
Northern Ireland's treasure house mixes Armada gold, Egyptian mummy Takabuti, Irish art and Troubles history beneath one brutalist-meets-classical roof in the Botanic Gardens.
SS Nomadic
The last surviving White Star Line vessel, Titanic's original tender, sits restored in Hamilton Dock, letting visitors walk decks once trodden by first-class passengers.
Crown Liquor Saloon
A gloriously ornate Victorian gin palace of etched glass, gaslights and carved snugs, so precious it is owned by the National Trust yet still pours pints.

train.note: The cross-border Enterprise runs roughly hourly from Belfast Grand Central to Dublin Connolly. No passport control on the land border (Common Travel Area), but non-Irish/UK citizens should carry their documents.

bus.note: Frequent cross-border coaches run from the Europa Buscentre and Glengall Street to Dublin city centre and Dublin Airport in about 2 hours. No passport control on the land border under the Common Travel Area, but non-Irish/UK citizens should carry documents.

ferry.note: Stena Line sails from Belfast to Cairnryan in south-west Scotland in about 2h15, several times daily; from Cairnryan it is a road connection onward to Glasgow. P&O Ferries run a parallel Larne-Cairnryan route just north of the city.

full.blurb: Ireland's capital just across the border, with Trinity College, Guinness Storehouse, and Georgian squares, reachable in about two hours.
full.name: Dublin

half.blurb: A grand Norman-revival castle and country estate with formal gardens and woodland trails on the shore of Strangford Lough.

half.blurb: A well-preserved 17th-century walled city with a scenic circuit atop the ramparts and rich history, about 1h15 from Belfast.
